11.text: Dolls. — Some of the dolls with which the girls

12.text: play are used also as charms to procure future fer-

13.text: tility for their owners. Such dolls pass from mother

14.text: to daughter, and are kept carefully patched and

15.text: mended, so as to last for an indefinite time. The bride

16.text: brings this doll to her new house, and keeps it in

17.text: her bag. In due time she gives it to her oldest

18.text: daughter to play with and to keep. When other

19.text: daughters are born, a little stuffing is taken out of

20.text: the hereditary doll and put into a new one, which

21.text: is then supposed to possess all the qualities of the

22.text: first doll. Dolls of this kind are usually shaped like

23.text: new-born babies. Incantations are recited over them

24.text: by each generation, so that their force is supposed to increase continually.¹

25.text: The peculiar feature of this kind of charm is, that it passes in the female

26.text: line, and therefore continually changes from one family to another. The

27.text: Chukchee women value such dolls highly. In the Kolyma country, when

28.text: stopping for a night in a Chukchee tent, I bought an hereditary doll from

29.text: the mistress. On the second day, after we had gone a long distance, the

30.text: woman suddenly changed her mind and started to overtake us, so that she

31.text: might return the price and recover her heirloom. She found us in a camp
